title: A Star Crash Glowed in X-Rays for Nearly 10 Minutes
summary:
Astronomers have long used short flashes of gamma rays to spot crashes between neutron stars. Neutron stars are very dense stellar remnants left behind after massive stars reach the end of their lives. When two of them merge, they send gravitational waves traveling through space. The gamma-ray flash from a merger can vanish in less than two seconds.

This time, one event lasted much longer in X-rays. On July 4, 2025, three satellites detected an event called EP250704a. Its gamma-ray burst lasted only about half a second. But the Einstein Probe, a satellite launched in January 2024, recorded bright X-rays for nearly ten minutes.

Researchers in Professor Eleonora Troja's group concluded that they may have witnessed the formation of a magnetar. A magnetar is a rapidly spinning neutron star with a huge magnetic field. Troja said that a magnetar can make an explosion brighter and longer-lasting.

After the Einstein Probe sent an alert, the team quickly organized follow-up observations with several instruments, including the Very Large Telescope in Chile. Graduate student Niccolò Passaleva responded within minutes. He was traveling home by train, but he took charge of one of the largest telescopes in the world from his laptop. "This is the longest lasting prompt X-ray flash ever observed from a neutron star merger," Passaleva said.

The team also measured how far away the flash was. Its light traveled for more than six billion years before reaching Earth. That means the explosion happened long before our Sun and its planets formed.

The researchers had spent several years looking for a firm link between this kind of X-ray flash and neutron star mergers. Earlier candidates faded too quickly. The new study presents strong evidence for that link.
why_it_matters: It helps scientists learn how some of the strangest flashes in space are made, and shows how fast teamwork can catch a rare event.
